title: Approval of 2022 audited financial statements
subtitle: Clean audit opinion, declining reserves, asset consumption, grant reliance, investment options and infrastructure renewal funding
overview: Council held a special meeting to review and approve the City of Guelph's 2022 Consolidated Financial Statements and the external audit findings report. Council approved them {{vote:m1}}. The auditor, KPMG, gave a clean opinion with no qualifications, no corrected or uncorrected errors and no control deficiencies identified.

Staff explained that the statements use full accrual accounting. That is why the surplus differs from the budget reports council saw in May. Staff said the city's debt ratios meet targets, but reserve ratios have started to decline, especially capital reserve funds and tax-supported contingency reserves. Assets are also more used up than a year earlier, though capital spending on assets rose in 2022.

This matters to residents because the statements show the city's overall financial health and the pressure on funding for aging infrastructure. Staff expect to bring updated recommendations in the next multi-year budget cycle. The auditor also noted that new accounting rules for asset retirement obligations will affect next year's statements, possibly significantly.

decisions.detail: Council approved the City of Guelph 2022 Consolidated Financial Statements and the External Audit Findings Report dated June 14, 2023.

debate: Councillors asked about the asset consumption ratio and reserves. Staff said the ratio should begin to reverse as the backlog of capital projects is completed and renewal investment continues, and that a capital plan resourcing strategy was introduced to address the trend.

Staff said the 2023 budget reduced infrastructure renewal tax funding and that the finance team will revisit this as the next budget is prepared. One councillor responded that the transfer was not cut but grew more slowly, and that it remained above $20 million.

One councillor asked whether planned drawdowns of reserves for projects such as the new library and south-end recreation centre would show up as a negative indicator. Staff said both cash and investments and reserve balances would fall, so the ratio should not be hurt.

A question on federal and provincial funding noted that the city has little control over it. Staff agreed that what the city receives depends on what is offered, but said the city actively seeks and applies for grants.

Staff said work continues on whether to move to the prudent investor standard, which would allow a wider range of investments under a different governance structure. A report is expected later this year or early next year.
